entry: Medieval style of art, emerging in northern France in the early 12th century. It developed out of [[Romanesque art]] alongside [[Gothic architecture]] and spread across [[Western Europe]] and much of Central Europe, never quite effacing more classical styles in Italy. Primary media were sculpture, panel painting, stained glass, fresco and illuminated manuscripts. The earliest works were monumental sculptures on cathedral and abbey walls. Christian art was often typological, showing scenes from the [[Old Testament]] beside those of the [[New Testament]]. Images of the Virgin Mary became more human and affectionate. As cities, universities and trade grew, secular art flourished, and artists were often required to join [[Guild|guilds]], so more of them are known by name than in any earlier period.

Literary genre of fear and haunting, often called Gothic horror. Its name comes from the Renaissance-era pejorative use of gothic, meaning medieval and barbaric. Horace Walpole's *The Castle of Otranto* (1764) was the first work labelled Gothic. Typical elements include ruined castles, the threat of supernatural events, persecution and the intrusion of the past upon the present. Later writers such as [[Mary Shelley]] and [[Walter Scott]] drew on its motifs, and [[Edgar Allan Poe]] and [[Bram Stoker]] extended it into the 19th century and beyond.

Germanic people who played a major role in the [[Fall of the Western Roman Empire|fall of the Western Roman Empire]]. First mentioned by Greco-Roman authors in the 3rd century AD, they lived north of the [[Danube]] in what is now Ukraine, Moldova and Romania. Goth-led forces defeated the Romans at the Battle of Adrianople in 378. In 410 a group led by [[Alaric I]] sacked Rome; these were precursors of the [[Visigoths]], who later established a [[Visigothic Kingdom]] in Spain. Ostrogoths under [[Theodoric the Great]] ruled Italy from Ravenna until Byzantium destroyed their kingdom in the 6th century. A Gothic culture in Crimea survived for more than a thousand years, though the Goths eventually ceased to exist as a distinct people. [[Gothic architecture]] and Gothic literature take their names from the Goths, though the Goths did not create or influence them.

German polymath, mathematician and philosopher. Alongside [[Isaac Newton]], he is credited with inventing [[Calculus|calculus]], and his notation became the conventional form. He is also credited with devising the modern [[Binary number|binary number system]] that underlies digital computing, and he made foundational contributions to statistics and binary arithmetic. A pioneer of mechanical calculators, he invented the Leibniz wheel, later used in the arithmometer, the first mass-produced mechanical calculator. As a philosopher he was a leading [[Rationalism|rationalist]] who argued that ours is, in a qualified sense, the best possible world God could have created, a view mocked by [[Voltaire]] in *Candide*. Born in [[Leipzig]], he wrote mainly in Latin, French and German.

German Enlightenment philosopher, dramatist and critic. Widely considered the first dramaturg, he worked at the Hamburg National Theatre, where his *Hamburg Dramaturgy* (1767–69) is the work in which the word "dramaturgy" first appears. His plays and theoretical writings substantially influenced [[German literature]]. His treatise *Laocoön* (1766) distinguished poetry from the visual arts by their spatial and temporal dimensions. From 1770 he was librarian at the ducal library in Wolfenbüttel, where in 1773 he discovered [[Archimedes|Archimedes']] cattle problem in a Greek manuscript. His play *Nathan the Wise* (1779) exemplified tolerance through a parable equating [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]], and it drew censorship and criticism.

German philosopher, logician and mathematician. Often considered the father of [[Analytic philosophy]], he concentrated on the [[Philosophy of language|philosophy of language]], [[Logic|logic]] and mathematics. He developed modern logic in *Begriffsschrift*, and in *The Foundations of Arithmetic* he argued for logicism, the thesis that [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]] derives from logic. Largely ignored in his lifetime, he was introduced to later philosophers by [[Bertrand Russell]] and, to some extent, [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]]. Frege is widely considered one of the greatest logicians since [[Aristotle]]. In "On Sense and Reference" he argued for two different kinds of meaning, sense and reference.

Form of [[Arthritis|arthritis]] caused by excess uric acid in the blood. Gout causes recurrent attacks of a painful, red, hot, swollen joint, reaching maximum intensity in less than 12 hours. The base of the big toe is affected in about half of cases. Uric acid crystals deposit in joints, tendons and surrounding tissues, and risk rises with diets rich in meat and [[Seafood|seafood]], [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] and sugar-sweetened drinks, and with obesity. Treatment uses nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, glucocorticoids or colchicine, while allopurinol or probenecid provides long-term prevention for those with frequent attacks. Gout affects about 1–5% of adults in the developed world at some point, and older men are most commonly affected. Historically called "the disease of kings", it has been recognized since at least the time of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]].

National authority of the [[India|Republic of India]], established under the [[Constitution of India]]. It is a parliamentary republic in which the [[Head of state|president]] is head of state and the prime minister, as [[Head of government|head of government]], leads the Union Council of Ministers. The government has three branches: the legislature, the [[Executive (government)|executive]] and the [[Judiciary]]. Parliament is bicameral and sits in [[New Delhi]]. India is divided into 28 states and eight union territories under a quasi-federal system.

Major seaport and most populous city of the Eastern Cape province of [[South Africa]]. Founded in 1820 as Port Elizabeth by Sir Rufane Donkin, governor of the Cape, it was established to strengthen the border between the Cape Colony and the Xhosa. It was renamed Gqeberha, after the Xhosa name for the Baakens River, with the change gazetted on 23 February 2021. Lying on the western shore of Algoa Bay, it is 770 km east of [[Cape Town]] and faces the [[Indian Ocean]]. Its deepwater harbor supports a major automotive industry. Known for blue-flag beaches and as a gateway for safari tourism, it is the sixth-most populous city in South Africa.

Ancient Roman tribunes of the plebs, brothers known for social reform. Tiberius Gracchus, tribune in 133 BC, passed legislation establishing a commission to survey public land and redistribute it to poor rural farmers. His brother Gaius Gracchus, tribune in 122–121 BC, extended these agrarian reforms and started colonization outside Italy; his reforms were far broader, also touching on provincial commands and jury composition. Both brothers were killed during or shortly after their tribunates, and the violence set a dangerous precedent that force was acceptable against political enemies. The Gracchi were later portrayed as social revolutionaries in the [[French Revolution]] and inspired opposition to [[Enclosure|enclosure]] in Britain. Recent scholarship views their agrarian reforms as less impactful than the ancient sources claim.

American computer scientist and United States Navy rear admiral. A pioneer of computer programming, she devised the theory of machine-independent [[Programming language|programming languages]] and developed FLOW-MATIC, a major influence on [[COBOL]]. She was one of the first programmers on the Harvard Mark I, is credited with writing the first computer manual, and is often credited with creating the first [[Compiler|compiler]]. After a Ph.D. in mathematics from [[Yale University]] and teaching at Vassar College, she joined the Navy Reserve during World War II. In 1949 she joined the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation, where she worked on UNIVAC I. In 1959 she helped create COBOL through the CODASYL consortium. She received the National Medal of Technology in 1991 and was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

Jamaican singer, songwriter, model and actress. She began as a fashion model in New York and Paris and became one of the most prominent Black models of the 1970s. From 1977 she was associated with the [[Disco|disco]] scene around New York's Studio 54, where she was called "Disco Queen". In the early 1980s she moved toward a new wave style drawing on [[Reggae]], [[Funk]] and pop. Her acting roles included *Conan the Destroyer* (1984) and May Day in the [[James Bond]] film *A View to a Kill* (1985). She earned another [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] nomination for her featured role on *Renaissance* (2022) by [[Beyoncé]].

American actress and princess consort of [[Monaco]]. Her films include *High Noon* (1952) and *Mogambo* (1953), and she won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *The Country Girl* (1954). She made three thrillers with [[Alfred Hitchcock]], among them *Rear Window* (1954). She retired from acting at 26 to marry Prince Rainier III in 1956. As princess she focused on children and the arts, founding the Princess Grace Foundation in 1964. Her children's rights organization, AMADE Mondiale, gained consultative status with [[UNICEF]] and [[UNESCO]].

Concept in [[Christianity]] of God's unearned favor and gift. In Western belief, grace is God's favor and "a share in the divine life of God", which cannot be earned and manifests most in the salvation of sinners. In the Eastern Orthodox Church, grace is the uncreated energies of God. Catholics, Eastern Orthodox and Protestants agree that grace is a gift from God. The Catholic Church holds that the sacraments confer the grace they signify, and John Wesley called the [[Eucharist]] the "grand channel" through which grace reaches believers. Calvinists teach irresistible grace, which regenerates only those predestined to salvation, while [[Arminianism|Arminians]] see grace cooperating with free will. [[Augustine of Hippo]] defended the necessity of grace against Pelagianism in the fifth century, an emphasis that influenced [[John Calvin]] and the [[Reformation]].

Vector field giving the direction and rate of fastest increase of a scalar function. For a differentiable function of several variables, the gradient ∇f is the vector of [[Partial derivative|partial derivatives]] in [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]]. The direction of the gradient is the direction in which the function increases most quickly, and its magnitude is the rate of that increase. The nabla symbol ∇ is pronounced "del". The property underlies [[Gradient descent]], an optimization technique widely used in [[Machine learning]].

First-order iterative algorithm for minimizing a differentiable multivariate function. It takes repeated steps opposite to the [[Gradient|gradient]] at the current point, the direction of steepest descent; stepping along the gradient instead is gradient ascent. Generally attributed to [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], who first suggested it in 1847, the method is widely used in [[Machine learning]] and [[Artificial intelligence]] to minimize cost or loss functions. Its stochastic extension is the most basic algorithm for training most [[Deep learning|deep networks]] today.

Writing or drawings made on a surface, usually without permission and in public view. Graffiti has existed since ancient times, with examples in [[Ancient Egypt]], [[Ancient Greece]] and the [[Roman Empire]]. The Alexamenos graffito, a Roman example that may contain one of the earliest depictions of [[Jesus]], was later seen as blasphemous and removed. Modern graffiti began in the [[New York City Subway|New York City subway system]] and in [[Philadelphia]] in the early 1970s, and spread worldwide. In most countries, marking property without permission is considered vandalism. Graffiti is distinguished from [[Mural|murals]], an often legally permitted form of street art.

Irish comedian, broadcaster and chat show host. Born Graham William Walker, he is best known for presenting *The Graham Norton Show* on the [[BBC]] since 2007. He has won a record six British Academy Television Awards for Best Entertainment Performance. Since 2009 he has been the BBC's television commentator for the final of the [[Eurovision Song Contest]]. Raised in Bandon, County Cork, he was the son of a sales representative for [[Guinness]]. In 2012 he sold his production company So Television to ITV for around £17 million.

American singer-songwriter and guitarist. Born Ingram Cecil Connor III, he recorded with the International Submarine Band, the Byrds and the Flying Burrito Brothers. He popularized what he called "Cosmic American Music", a hybrid of country, [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]], soul, folk and [[Rock and roll|rock]]. He is credited with helping to found country rock and alt-country. He was ranked No. 87 on [[Rolling Stone]] magazine's list of the 100 Greatest Artists of All Time. He was posthumously inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2026, in the musical influence category.

[[Grammar|Grammatical]] category expressing time reference, usually marked on verbs. Tense places an action or state relative to the moment of speaking, typically as past, present or future. Some languages have only two tenses, such as past and nonpast, and most [[Chinese language|Chinese languages]] are tenseless, conveying time through context and other means. Relative tense places events relative to a point established in discourse, as with the pluperfect ("past-in-the-past"). Tense is often bound up with aspect and mood, and some languages have a single tense–aspect–mood system. The English word derives from Old French *tens*, from [[Latin]] *tempus*, "time".

American awards for achievement in music, presented by the Recording Academy. Often called the Grammys, they are one of four major annual American entertainment awards, alongside the [[Academy Awards]], Emmy and Tony awards. The idea arose in a 1950s project related to the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]], and the name recalls the gramophone invented by [[Emile Berliner]]. The first ceremony was held on May 4, 1959. After more than fifty years on [[CBS]], the broadcast moved to ABC and Disney+ under a ten-year deal announced on October 30, 2024. The 68th ceremony, with 95 categories, was held on February 1, 2026.

Semiarid lowland region of central South America. Spanning over one million square kilometers across eastern Bolivia, western Paraguay, northern Argentina and parts of Brazil, it forms part of the [[Río de la Plata]] basin. Its mix of dry forests, thorn scrub, [[Savanna|savannas]] and [[Wetland|wetlands]] makes it the continent's second-largest forested ecoregion. It is home to more than 3,400 plant species, around 500 bird species and 150 mammals, including [[Jaguar|jaguars]]. [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous peoples]] including the Wichí, Qom, Pilagá, Guaraní and Ayoreo have sparsely inhabited the region for centuries. Cattle ranching, soybean farming and fire-driven clearing have caused extensive [[Deforestation|deforestation]]; Argentina alone lost about seven million hectares of forest between 1998 and 2023.

Republic in northern South America and parts of Central America, 1819–1831. Its territory covered [[Colombia|present-day Colombia]], mainland [[Ecuador]], [[Panama]], [[Venezuela]], and parts of northern [[Peru]] and northwestern Brazil. It was proclaimed at the Congress of Angostura in 1819 and took effect under the Constitution of Cúcuta (1821), which established a unitary centralist state. Its politics divided between [[Simón Bolívar]], who favored a strong presidency, and Vice-President Francisco de Paula Santander, who backed constitutional rule. Disputes over [[Federalism|federalism]] and centralism, along with regional tensions, led to its dissolution in 1831 into Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela. Panama was separated from Colombia in 1903.

City (pop., 2024: 233,532), capital of Granada province in [[Andalusia]], [[Spain]]. Located at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, it was the last Muslim stronghold in Islamic Spain, and the capital of the Nasrid emirate from the 13th century. The Catholic Monarchs, [[Ferdinand II of Aragon]] and [[Isabella I of Castile]], conquered it in 1492. Its [[Alhambra]], a Nasrid citadel and palace, is one of the most visited sites in Spain and one of the most famous monuments of [[Islamic architecture]]. The [[Pomegranate|pomegranate]] is its heraldic device. The University of Granada has an estimated 47,000 undergraduate students across five campuses.

Post-harvest storage building for grain or seeds, usually raised above the ground. Granaries protect stored grain from [[Rodent|rodents]], pests, [[Flood|floods]] and bad weather, and they help dry grain to prevent mold. The oldest known granaries date to 9500 BC in the Jordan Valley. In [[Ancient Egypt]], grain was stored against years of scarcity. In the South Hams of southwest [[Great Britain]], small granaries were built on mushroom-shaped stumps called staddle stones. Historically a [[Silo|silo]] was a pit for grain, distinct from the above-ground granary. Modern granaries may use ventilation and temperature control to preserve grain quality, and modern grain farms often use steel granaries.
